[SECTION 6: NON-SOLICITATION OF EMPLOYEES]{.underline}**

**6.1 Preferred Position**

**Mutual non-solicitation** of employees for a period of **twelve (12) months** following the termination or expiration of the NDA.

**Exception:** General advertisements (e.g., job postings on public websites, job boards, or in newspapers of general circulation) and responses to unsolicited inquiries from the other party\'s employees shall not constitute \"solicitation\" for purposes of this restriction.

**Commentary:** Employee non-solicitation protects Stonebridge\'s significant investment in its technical workforce --- particularly engineers and scientists with specialized knowledge of micro-needle fabrication, embedded firmware systems, biocompatible materials, and predictive dosing algorithms. Given Stonebridge\'s relatively small workforce of approximately 1,400 employees, the loss of even a few key technical personnel to a counterparty could significantly impact ongoing R&D programs and delay product development timelines. Mutuality is essential: Stonebridge should not accept restrictions on its own hiring that do not equally apply to the counterparty. Non-solicitation provisions that burden Stonebridge unilaterally are fundamentally one-sided and commercially unacceptable.

**6.2 Acceptable Range**

> • **Mutual non-solicitation** for a period of **six (6) to eighteen (18) months** following termination or expiration.
>
> • **Exception for both general advertisements and unsolicited inquiries** --- that is, situations where the counterparty\'s employee independently initiates contact with Stonebridge (or vice versa) without solicitation.

**Commentary:** Durations shorter than six months provide minimal practical protection, as the period is too brief to deter targeted recruitment efforts by a counterparty that has gained insight into Stonebridge\'s workforce during the NDA relationship. Durations of up to eighteen months are commercially reasonable and generally enforceable across most U.S. jurisdictions. Always ensure the general advertising exception is included --- without it, the provision could be challenged as an unreasonable restraint on trade and may also create compliance risk for Stonebridge\'s Human Resources department, which regularly posts open positions on public job boards and company websites. Any duration and structure within this range may be accepted without escalation.

**6.3 Unacceptable / Escalate**

> • **Non-solicitation period exceeding twenty-four (24) months.** Periods of this length are likely unenforceable in many jurisdictions and are commercially unreasonable for a standard NDA relationship. Courts frequently scrutinize the reasonableness of non-solicitation periods, and an excessive duration may result in the entire provision being struck as an unreasonable restraint.
>
> • **Unilateral non-solicitation** that restricts only Stonebridge from soliciting the counterparty\'s employees while the counterparty remains free to solicit Stonebridge employees. This is a fundamentally one-sided restriction that provides no reciprocal benefit to Stonebridge and should never be accepted.
>
> • **Non-solicitation with no exception for general advertisements.** An overly broad provision that treats public job postings as \"solicitation\" is commercially unworkable. Stonebridge posts hundreds of open positions annually on its website, LinkedIn, and various job boards. A non-solicitation clause that captures these general postings would impose impossible compliance obligations on the HR department and expose Stonebridge to breach claims based on routine hiring activities.

**Commentary:** A unilateral non-solicitation clause is never acceptable. If a counterparty proposes a non-solicitation provision, it must be mutual. If the counterparty refuses mutuality, Stonebridge should propose deleting the non-solicitation provision entirely rather than accepting a one-sided restriction. Additionally, any duration exceeding eighteen months should be negotiated down to the preferred twelve-month period or, at minimum, into the acceptable range. Any clause lacking a general advertising exception should be immediately redlined to add the standard carve-out. If a counterparty insists on terms that fall into the \"Unacceptable\" category on any of these dimensions, escalate to General Counsel.

**[SECTION 7: GOVERNING LAW AND DISPUTE RESOLUTION]{.underline}**

**7.1 Preferred Position**

**Governing Law:** The laws of the State of **Delaware**, without regard to conflicts-of-law principles that would require the application of the laws of any other jurisdiction.

**Forum:** Exclusive jurisdiction in the **Delaware Court of Chancery** or, if the Court of Chancery declines to exercise jurisdiction, the **United States District Court for the District of Delaware**.

**Commentary:** Stonebridge is incorporated in the State of Delaware. Delaware law is well-developed for commercial and contractual disputes, and Delaware courts --- particularly the Court of Chancery --- are highly regarded for their efficiency, expertise, and extensive body of precedent on commercial matters. Stonebridge\'s outside counsel at Northgate Whitford LLP has significant Delaware litigation experience and maintains relationships with local Delaware counsel for any matters requiring admission to the Delaware bar. Delaware\'s body of case law provides predictability and reduces the risk of unexpected outcomes in contractual interpretation disputes.

**7.2 Acceptable Range**

> • **Governing Law:** The laws of the State of **New York**, with exclusive jurisdiction in state or federal courts located in the Borough of Manhattan, City of New York. New York law is a standard fallback for commercial agreements and is well-developed for the types of disputes that may arise under NDAs.
>
> • **Alternative:** The law of the **disclosing party\'s home state** (which would mean Delaware law when Stonebridge is the disclosing party), with binding arbitration under the **American Arbitration Association (AAA) Commercial Arbitration Rules**, with the arbitral seat in a neutral U.S. city (e.g., Chicago, Illinois; Denver, Colorado; or another mutually agreed location within the continental United States).

**Commentary:** New York law provides a well-understood legal framework with an extensive body of commercial law precedent. AAA arbitration in a U.S. city provides a familiar, efficient dispute resolution mechanism that is widely accepted in the medical device and life sciences industries. Either alternative is acceptable without escalation, though the reviewing attorney should note the deviation from the Delaware preference in the matter file.

**7.3 Unacceptable / Escalate**

> • **Foreign governing law**, including but not limited to German law, English law, Swiss law, French law, Japanese law, or any other non-U.S. law. Foreign governing law creates significant uncertainty for Stonebridge. U.S. counsel may lack expertise in the applicable foreign law, requiring engagement of local counsel at additional cost. Foreign legal systems may have different default rules regarding implied licenses, trade secret protection, and the availability of injunctive relief, which could undermine the protections Stonebridge expects from the NDA.
>
> • **Foreign arbitral seat**, including but not limited to Zurich, London, Geneva, Munich, Singapore, Hong Kong, or any other non-U.S. city. Foreign arbitral seats impose logistical burdens, significantly increase costs, and may result in awards that are more difficult to enforce in U.S. courts. While the New York Convention provides a framework for enforcement of foreign arbitral awards, practical obstacles remain.
>
> • **ICC International Court of Arbitration** --- ICC proceedings are typically more expensive and time-consuming than AAA arbitration. ICC arbitration is often paired with a foreign arbitral seat and foreign governing law, compounding the concerns identified above. The administrative costs of ICC proceedings are significantly higher than those of AAA, and the timeline from filing to award is typically longer.
>
> • **Any dispute resolution mechanism** that requires resolution of disputes **outside the United States**, whether through litigation, arbitration, mediation, or any other process.

**Commentary:** Foreign governing law and non-U.S. dispute resolution are firm negotiation points. This is particularly important in the context of NDAs protecting Stonebridge\'s core intellectual property --- the enforceability of trade secret protections, the availability of injunctive relief, and the scope of implied license doctrines all vary significantly across jurisdictions. If a counterparty insists on foreign law or a foreign forum, escalate to General Counsel immediately. In cross-border transactions, Stonebridge may propose a compromise of New York law (as an internationally recognized neutral U.S. jurisdiction) with AAA arbitration seated in a major U.S. city, but should not agree to any non-U.S. forum under any circumstances absent General Counsel approval. Such approval would be exceptional and would require a documented risk acceptance memorandum.

**[SECTION 8: INJUNCTIVE RELIEF]{.underline}**

**8.1 Preferred Position**

The NDA should contain an express acknowledgment by both parties that a breach or threatened breach of the confidentiality obligations set forth in the NDA may cause **irreparable harm** to the disclosing party for which monetary damages would be an inadequate remedy. The NDA should further provide that, in the event of any such breach or threatened breach, the disclosing party shall be entitled to seek **injunctive or equitable relief** --- including temporary restraining orders, preliminary injunctions, and specific performance --- in any court of competent jurisdiction, **without the requirement of posting a bond or other security** and without the necessity of proving actual damages. This right to seek injunctive relief shall be in addition to (and not in lieu of) any other rights or remedies available at law or in equity.

**Commentary:** Trade secret misappropriation and confidentiality breaches are inherently difficult to remedy with money damages alone. Once proprietary information is disclosed to an unauthorized third party or made public, the competitive harm may be irreversible --- the proverbial bell cannot be unrung. The bond waiver is an important element because bond requirements can delay the grant of injunctive relief and impose a significant financial burden at a moment of crisis. Express acknowledgment of irreparable harm avoids the need to litigate this threshold issue in an emergency hearing, where speed is essential. Courts generally give weight to contractual stipulations of irreparable harm, though they retain discretion to evaluate the equities in any specific case.

**8.2 Acceptable Range**

> • **Injunctive relief clause without the bond waiver** --- that is, standard injunctive relief language that acknowledges irreparable harm and the right to seek equitable remedies but does not address bond requirements.

**Commentary:** Even without a bond waiver, an express injunctive relief clause that includes the irreparable harm stipulation establishes the parties\' intent and may persuade a court to grant emergency relief more readily. The absence of a bond waiver is not ideal --- the reviewing attorney may need to post a bond if a court requires one --- but it does not fundamentally impair Stonebridge\'s ability to seek injunctive relief. This is an acceptable deviation from the preferred position.

**8.3 Unacceptable / Escalate**

> • **No injunctive relief clause in the NDA.** The complete absence of an injunctive relief provision leaves Stonebridge without a contractual basis for arguing irreparable harm and without a clear pathway to equitable relief in the event of a breach. While Stonebridge would still have common law remedies, the lack of a contractual stipulation may slow the process at a critical juncture.
>
> • **Requirement to prove actual damages before seeking injunctive relief.** This is inconsistent with fundamental equitable principles and would effectively eliminate injunctive relief as a practical remedy. By the time actual damages can be proven, the information may have been widely disseminated, rendering the injunction moot.
>
> • **Mandatory arbitration as the sole remedy for all disputes, including confidentiality breaches, without a carve-out permitting either party to seek injunctive relief in a court of competent jurisdiction.** Arbitral tribunals may not be constituted quickly enough to address emergency breaches --- the process of selecting arbitrators, establishing jurisdiction, and scheduling hearings can take weeks or months. Interim measures issued by arbitrators may not be directly enforceable without court action, and some arbitral institutions do not have expedited procedures for emergency relief. A mandatory arbitration clause that channels all disputes exclusively through arbitration, with no exception for applications for temporary restraining orders or preliminary injunctions in a court of competent jurisdiction, effectively strips Stonebridge of its most important enforcement tool during the critical early hours and days following a breach.

**Commentary:** The arbitration carve-out issue frequently arises in NDAs that include an arbitration clause. If the NDA includes a mandatory arbitration mechanism, the reviewing attorney must ensure that there is an express carve-out stating that either party may seek interim or injunctive relief in a court of competent jurisdiction notwithstanding the arbitration provision, and that such court action shall not be deemed a waiver of the right to arbitrate the underlying merits of the dispute. This is a critical protection --- escalate immediately if absent. The carve-out should be drafted to apply to both parties (mutual) and should specify that the court may grant interim relief pending the constitution of the arbitral tribunal and the commencement of arbitration proceedings.

**[SECTION 9: RETURN / DESTRUCTION OF MATERIALS]{.underline}**

**9.1 Preferred Position**

Upon written request by the disclosing party or upon expiration or termination of the NDA (whichever is earlier), the receiving party must **return or destroy** all Confidential Information, including all copies, extracts, notes, summaries, and derivative materials, within **fifteen (15) business days** of such request or the date of expiration or termination.

The receiving party must provide a **written certification of destruction** signed by an **officer** of the receiving party, confirming that all Confidential Information in the receiving party\'s possession, custody, or control has been returned to the disclosing party or destroyed in accordance with the NDA\'s requirements.

**Exception for Legally Required Retention:** The receiving party may retain copies of Confidential Information solely to the extent required by applicable law, regulation, or the receiving party\'s established document-retention policies that apply to the receiving party\'s own records generally, **provided** that any such retained copies remain subject to the confidentiality obligations of the NDA for the full duration of the survival period specified in the NDA. The receiving party must identify in its certification any categories of Confidential Information being retained under this exception and the basis for such retention.

**Commentary:** The fifteen-business-day period provides appropriate urgency while being practically achievable for most organizations. Officer-level certification ensures accountability and seniority of oversight --- it imposes personal reputational risk on a senior executive, which incentivizes compliance. The legally required retention exception is a reasonable concession that reflects the practical reality that many organizations have legal holds, regulatory retention requirements, or automated backup systems that may capture Confidential Information. However, the ongoing confidentiality obligation for retained copies is essential --- without it, the retention exception swallows the return/destruction rule and effectively permits indefinite, unrestricted retention.

**9.2 Acceptable Range**

> • **Return or destruction within thirty (30) calendar days** of written request or expiration/termination. This extended period is reasonable for counterparties with complex IT systems, distributed storage infrastructure, or multiple office locations where Confidential Information may reside.
>
> • **Certification by an authorized representative** of the receiving party (not necessarily an officer) --- for example, the receiving party\'s general counsel, chief compliance officer, or head of information security. The key requirement is that the certifying individual has sufficient authority and organizational visibility to confirm that the return/destruction process was thorough and complete.

**Commentary:** A thirty-calendar-day period is the outer boundary of what Stonebridge considers reasonable for routine return/destruction obligations. Certification by an authorized representative below the officer level is acceptable provided the individual holds a position of sufficient seniority and responsibility. The reviewing attorney should ensure that the certification requirement is not diluted to a mere self-serving statement by a junior employee without organizational accountability.

**9.3 Unacceptable / Escalate**

> • **No return or destruction obligation whatsoever.** An NDA that permits the receiving party to retain all Confidential Information indefinitely after the termination of the relationship provides no post-termination protection and is fundamentally inconsistent with the purpose of an NDA.
>
> • **Retention rights that go beyond archival copies required by law** --- for example, a general right to retain \"one copy for compliance purposes\" or \"one archival copy\" without specifying that such copy remains subject to the ongoing confidentiality obligations of the NDA. This creates a loophole that effectively permits indefinite, unrestricted retention of Confidential Information under the guise of compliance or record-keeping.
>
> • **Destruction period exceeding sixty (60) calendar days.** A period of ninety days or longer creates prolonged exposure risk and suggests that the receiving party does not have adequate systems in place to manage confidential materials. Excessive delay is disproportionate and commercially unreasonable for standard NDA relationships.
>
> • **No certification requirement.** Without a written certification of destruction, there is no assurance or accountability that the destruction has actually occurred. Stonebridge would have no documentary evidence that the receiving party complied with its return/destruction obligations, making enforcement of this provision practically impossible.

**Commentary:** The archival copy issue is a common negotiation point. Stonebridge should always insist that any retained archival copy remains subject to the NDA\'s confidentiality obligations for the full survival period. This ongoing obligation is the critical safeguard --- it ensures that even retained copies cannot be used, disclosed, or exploited for any purpose other than the receiving party\'s legal compliance. If the counterparty refuses to include this condition, escalate to General Counsel. Additionally, destruction periods in excess of sixty calendar days should be resisted and negotiated down. If the counterparty can articulate a specific operational reason for needing additional time (e.g., complex global IT infrastructure), the reviewing attorney may consider an extension up to sixty days, but anything beyond that requires escalation.

**[SECTION 10: INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY / OWNERSHIP]{.underline}**

**10.1 Preferred Position**

The NDA must contain an explicit statement that **no license** --- whether express or implied, by estoppel, or otherwise --- is granted under any **patent, copyright, trademark, or trade secret** by virtue of disclosing Confidential Information under the NDA.

The NDA should further contain an express statement that all Confidential Information remains the sole and exclusive property of the disclosing party and that the receiving party acquires no rights, title, or interest in or to any Confidential Information by virtue of its disclosure under the NDA.

**Commentary:** This clause is critical. Without it, a counterparty could argue that the act of disclosing technical information --- particularly in the context of a partnership evaluation or co-development discussion --- creates an implied license to use that information. Given Stonebridge\'s 87 active U.S. patents and trade secrets in micro-needle fabrication processes, biocompatible polymer formulations, and predictive dosing algorithms, an implied license theory --- however unlikely to succeed on the merits --- could be costly to litigate and could create significant business uncertainty during the pendency of any legal dispute. An express \"no license\" clause that enumerates the specific types of intellectual property forecloses this argument and provides Stonebridge with a clear contractual defense.

**10.2 Acceptable Range**

> • **General \"no license\" clause** that disclaims the grant of any license or rights, without listing specific IP types --- for example: \"Nothing in this Agreement shall be construed as granting, by implication, estoppel, or otherwise, any license or right under any intellectual property.\"

**Commentary:** While the preferred position is to enumerate patent, copyright, trademark, and trade secret, a general no-license clause is adequate for most purposes and is standard market practice. The general formulation covers all categories of intellectual property without the risk of an *ejusdem generis* interpretation that might limit the clause\'s scope to only the enumerated IP types. Either formulation --- enumerated or general --- is acceptable.

**10.3 Unacceptable / Escalate**

> • **Any clause that grants a license or option to license IP through the NDA** --- regardless of scope, conditionality, or consideration. An NDA is a confidentiality agreement, not a license agreement. Any license grant, however narrow or conditional, should be negotiated and documented in a separate intellectual property license agreement with appropriate terms, conditions, and consideration.
>
> • **Silence on IP ownership** --- that is, the NDA contains no provision whatsoever addressing intellectual property rights, ownership, or licensing. Silence creates ambiguity and potential exposure to implied license arguments, particularly under the laws of foreign jurisdictions that may have different default rules regarding implied licenses arising from the disclosure of confidential technical information. Under certain civil law systems, for example, the act of disclosing technical information in the context of a commercial negotiation may give rise to implied rights or equitable claims that would not exist under U.S. law. Silence on IP ownership in an NDA governed by such foreign law compounds this risk.

**Commentary:** If the counterparty\'s NDA is silent on IP ownership and licensing, the reviewing attorney should propose Stonebridge\'s standard \"no license\" language. This is typically a non-controversial addition --- most sophisticated counterparties will agree to include it, as it protects both parties equally. If the counterparty resists adding a \"no license\" clause, escalate to General Counsel, as such resistance may signal an intent to claim rights in disclosed information or may reflect a difference in the counterparty\'s understanding of the NDA\'s purpose. The resistance itself is a meaningful data point that warrants heightened scrutiny.

**[SECTION 11: REPRESENTATIVES]{.underline}**

**11.1 Preferred Position**

\"Representatives\" should be defined broadly to include the following categories of persons and entities:

> **Officers, directors, employees, agents, advisors (including legal, financial, and accounting advisors), consultants, and Affiliates (including parent and subsidiary entities).**

\"Affiliates\" should be defined as any entity that, directly or indirectly, controls, is controlled by, or is under common control with a party, where \"control\" means the direct or indirect ownership of fifty percent (50%) or more of the voting interests of the entity in question.

**Commentary:** Stonebridge\'s due diligence and transaction evaluation teams routinely include the following categories of external participants:

> • Outside legal counsel --- currently Northgate Whitford LLP (Minneapolis, MN), which provides legal analysis, regulatory review, and contract drafting support.
>
> • Financial advisors --- currently Harmon Steele & Associates, which provides financial modeling, valuation analysis, and transaction advisory services.
>
> • External accountants --- currently Clearview Accounting Group, which provides accounting diligence, tax analysis, and financial statement review.
>
> • Technical consultants --- engaged on a project-specific basis to evaluate counterparty technologies, manufacturing capabilities, and product specifications.

Additionally, Stonebridge may need to share Confidential Information with subsidiaries or affiliated entities involved in related R&D programs, manufacturing operations, or commercial activities. A narrow \"Representatives\" definition that excludes any of these categories would operationally impair Stonebridge\'s ability to evaluate a potential transaction comprehensively and efficiently. The preferred definition is therefore intentionally broad to encompass all persons and entities who may participate in the diligence process.

**11.2 Acceptable Range**

> • **Definition that covers employees and professional advisors** (legal, financial, and accounting) but requires **written notice** to the counterparty before disclosing Confidential Information to Affiliates.

**Commentary:** A notice requirement for affiliate disclosures is a reasonable compromise that provides the counterparty with visibility into the scope of disclosure while preserving Stonebridge\'s ability to share information within its corporate group. The reviewing attorney should ensure that the notice requirement is procedurally workable --- for example, written notice within a specified period before or after the affiliate disclosure, rather than a requirement for advance consent, which could delay time-sensitive information sharing.

**11.3 Unacceptable / Escalate**

> • **Definition that excludes Affiliates entirely.** This prevents Stonebridge from sharing Confidential Information with its own subsidiaries and parent entities, which is operationally unworkable for a company with a corporate family structure. Stonebridge may have subsidiaries involved in manufacturing, regulatory affairs, or related R&D that need access to Confidential Information received under the NDA.
>
> • **Definition that is limited solely to employees.** This excludes directors, officers, outside advisors, consultants, agents, and affiliates. Such a narrow definition would prevent Stonebridge from engaging its outside legal, financial, and accounting advisors in the diligence process --- a result that is fundamentally incompatible with Stonebridge\'s standard transaction practices.
>
> • **Definition limited to \"employees and in-house legal counsel.\"** While slightly broader than a definition limited solely to employees, this still excludes outside advisors, financial advisors, accountants, consultants, agents, and affiliates. Given Stonebridge\'s extensive reliance on external advisors --- including Northgate Whitford LLP, Harmon Steele & Associates, and Clearview Accounting Group --- this definition is functionally unacceptable. A counterparty\'s definition that includes in-house counsel but excludes outside counsel suggests either an unfamiliarity with standard NDA practice or an intentional effort to restrict Stonebridge\'s ability to obtain external advice and analysis.
>
> • **Definition that excludes agents and consultants.** Stonebridge periodically engages specialized technical consultants to evaluate counterparty technologies, including biomedical engineers, software auditors, and regulatory specialists who are not employees or traditional professional advisors. A definition that excludes these individuals creates gaps in Stonebridge\'s diligence capabilities.

**Commentary:** If the counterparty\'s definition is too narrow, the reviewing attorney should propose Stonebridge\'s broad definition as a replacement. If the counterparty objects to including affiliates, offer the notice-requirement compromise described in the \"Acceptable Range\" above. If the counterparty objects to including outside advisors, explain that such advisors are essential to Stonebridge\'s standard diligence process and that they will be bound by confidentiality obligations at least as protective as those in the NDA --- either through the NDA itself or through separate engagement agreements. This is a firm position --- escalate to General Counsel if the counterparty refuses to expand the definition to include, at minimum, employees, officers, directors, and professional advisors (legal, financial, and accounting).

**[SECTION 12: ASSIGNMENT]{.underline}**

**12.1 Preferred Position**

**No assignment** of the NDA or any rights or obligations thereunder without the prior written consent of the other party, such consent **not to be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed**.

**Automatic Assignment Exception:** Either party may assign the NDA without the other party\'s consent in connection with a **merger, acquisition, consolidation, or sale of all or substantially all of the assigning party\'s assets**, provided that the assignee expressly assumes all of the assigning party\'s obligations under the NDA in writing. The assigning party shall provide written notice to the non-assigning party within thirty (30) days of such assignment.

**Commentary:** The reasonableness qualifier on the consent requirement ensures that neither party can unreasonably block a legitimate assignment --- for example, an assignment to a successor entity following a corporate reorganization. The M&A carve-out is important because both Stonebridge and its counterparties may undergo corporate transactions during the NDA term, and requiring the other party\'s affirmative consent for such transactions could create deal uncertainty, delay closing timelines, or give the non-assigning party an undue veto right over a transformative corporate event. The written assumption requirement ensures that the assignee is contractually bound to the NDA\'s obligations, and the notice requirement provides transparency.

**12.2 Acceptable Range**

> • **No assignment without prior written consent**, with or without a reasonableness standard, provided the restriction applies **equally to both parties**. Even without a reasonableness qualifier, a mutual consent requirement is balanced because neither party is disadvantaged relative to the other.

**Commentary:** The key principle is symmetry. Whether or not the consent requirement includes a \"not to be unreasonably withheld\" qualifier is less important than ensuring that the same standard applies to both parties. An assignment provision that imposes different standards on the two parties --- for example, requiring one party to obtain consent while allowing the other to assign freely --- is inherently one-sided and should be treated as described in the \"Unacceptable / Escalate\" section below.

**12.3 Unacceptable / Escalate**

> • **Free assignability by the counterparty** --- that is, the counterparty may assign the NDA (including assignments of Stonebridge\'s Confidential Information to the assignee) without Stonebridge\'s consent, while Stonebridge requires the counterparty\'s consent to assign. This asymmetry is commercially one-sided and could result in Stonebridge\'s Confidential Information being transferred to an entity with which Stonebridge has no relationship and no desire to share proprietary information.
>
> • **Unilateral assignment rights** --- any arrangement where the counterparty has broader assignment rights than Stonebridge. This includes M&A or affiliate assignment carve-outs that apply only to the counterparty but not to Stonebridge. For example, if the counterparty reserves the right to assign the NDA to any affiliate without consent, the same right must be available to Stonebridge. A unilateral carve-out means that the counterparty could assign Stonebridge\'s Confidential Information to an acquirer, affiliate, or successor entity without Stonebridge\'s consent, while Stonebridge cannot do the same. This is commercially unacceptable.
>
> • **Assignment to competitors.** If the NDA includes an M&A assignment carve-out, the reviewing attorney should consider whether the carve-out should include a restriction preventing assignment to a direct competitor of Stonebridge without Stonebridge\'s consent. While this additional restriction is not part of Stonebridge\'s standard template, it may be appropriate in circumstances where the counterparty\'s M&A activity could result in Stonebridge\'s Confidential Information being held by a competitor.

**Commentary:** Assignment provisions must be symmetric. If a counterparty includes an M&A or affiliate assignment carve-out for itself, the same carve-out must apply to Stonebridge. If the counterparty refuses mutuality, the reviewing attorney should propose that the carve-out be deleted for both parties --- reverting to a mutual consent-required standard --- rather than accepting a one-sided arrangement. Escalate to General Counsel if the counterparty insists on asymmetric assignment rights.

**[SECTION 13: REMEDIES AND INDEMNIFICATION]{.underline}**

**13.1 Preferred Position**

**Mutual Indemnification:** Each party shall indemnify, defend, and hold harmless the other party and its officers, directors, employees, and agents from and against all losses, damages, liabilities, costs, and expenses (including reasonable attorneys\' fees and costs of litigation or arbitration) arising from or related to a breach of the NDA by the indemnifying party or its Representatives.

**No Cap on Liability:** There should be no cap on liability for breach of confidentiality obligations under the NDA.

**Commentary:** Mutual indemnification is standard for bilateral NDAs and ensures both parties have a clear contractual remedy in the event of a breach. The absence of a liability cap for confidentiality breaches is critical because the damages from a trade secret leak, unauthorized disclosure of regulatory data, or a data breach involving proprietary algorithms can be disproportionately large and difficult to quantify at the time the NDA is executed. A low cap --- or any cap at all --- could leave Stonebridge dramatically under-compensated in the event of a material breach. The indemnification should be mutual to reflect the bilateral nature of the NDA and the fact that both parties are exchanging confidential information.

**13.2 Acceptable Range**

> • **No indemnification clause** --- standard for many NDAs. In the absence of an indemnification provision, the parties rely on common law breach-of-contract and tort remedies, including claims for trade secret misappropriation under the Defend Trade Secrets Act and applicable state law.
>
> • **No limitation of liability clause** --- silence on liability limitations is acceptable and preserves Stonebridge\'s full range of legal remedies without any contractual cap or restriction.

**Commentary:** Many NDAs omit both indemnification and limitation-of-liability provisions entirely. This is commercially neutral and acceptable for Stonebridge. The important consideration is that there be no affirmative limitation that restricts Stonebridge\'s remedies below what would otherwise be available under applicable law. Silence on both points is preferable to a one-sided indemnification or an unfavorable liability cap.

**13.3 Unacceptable / Escalate**

> • **Liability cap applicable to confidentiality breaches.** Any cap on liability for breaches of confidentiality is unacceptable, regardless of the cap amount. A liability cap effectively pre-discounts the cost of a breach and may incentivize inadequate safeguards on the part of the receiving party. Whether the cap is set at one million dollars or one hundred million dollars, it creates a ceiling on exposure that is fundamentally inconsistent with the open-ended nature of the harm that can result from unauthorized disclosure of trade secrets, patent applications, or proprietary manufacturing data.
>
> • **Consequential damages waiver applicable to confidentiality breaches.** Most damages arising from confidentiality breaches --- including lost competitive advantage, lost business opportunities, diminished patent value, increased time-to-market for competing products, and erosion of trade secret status --- are inherently consequential in nature. A waiver of consequential damages for confidentiality breaches would eliminate the most significant category of recoverable loss and leave Stonebridge with little more than direct out-of-pocket costs, which are often minimal relative to the true competitive harm.
>
> • **Unilateral indemnification favoring the counterparty** --- that is, only Stonebridge indemnifies the counterparty for breaches, but the counterparty does not indemnify Stonebridge. This is one-sided and unacceptable in a bilateral NDA where both parties are disclosing and receiving Confidential Information.

**Commentary:** If a counterparty insists on a general limitation of liability or consequential damages waiver --- which is common in broader commercial agreements and may be included as boilerplate --- Stonebridge should insist on a **carve-out** that expressly excludes breaches of confidentiality obligations from the scope of the cap and/or waiver. This carve-out approach is widely accepted in the market and allows the counterparty to retain its general limitation of liability for other claims while preserving Stonebridge\'s full remedies for confidentiality breaches. This is a firm position. If the counterparty refuses to include the carve-out, escalate to General Counsel immediately. The General Counsel will evaluate whether the overall transaction justifies acceptance of the limitation, but acceptance should be the rare exception rather than the rule.

**[SECTION 14: NO OBLIGATION TO TRANSACT]{.underline}**

**14.1 Preferred Position**

The NDA should contain an express statement that the NDA **does not obligate either party** to enter into any further agreement, transaction, or business relationship of any kind.

The NDA should further state that either party may terminate discussions, negotiations, and evaluations at any time, for any reason or no reason, without liability to the other party (except for obligations arising under the NDA itself, which shall survive termination in accordance with the NDA\'s terms).

**Commentary:** This is a fundamental principle of NDA practice. An NDA is an agreement to protect information exchanged during a pre-transaction evaluation --- it is not a commitment to pursue or consummate any particular transaction. Without this clause, a counterparty might argue that the NDA created an implied obligation to negotiate in good faith, to pursue a specific transaction, or to refrain from pursuing alternative opportunities. An express \"no obligation\" clause forecloses these arguments and preserves each party\'s freedom of action. This clause should appear in every NDA Stonebridge executes, whether inbound or outbound.

**14.2 Acceptable Range**

> • **Implied through the overall structure of the NDA** --- that is, the NDA is clearly limited to confidentiality protections and does not contain any affirmative transaction obligations, exclusivity provisions, or standstill restrictions. In such cases, the absence of an express \"no obligation\" clause is not necessarily problematic if the NDA\'s scope is unambiguous.

**Commentary:** While the absence of an express \"no obligation\" clause is not automatically a deficiency if the NDA is otherwise clean, Stonebridge\'s strong preference is to include an express statement. An express clause eliminates ambiguity, provides clear contractual language to point to in the event of a dispute, and is standard market practice for NDAs in the medical device and life sciences sectors. The reviewing attorney should propose adding Stonebridge\'s standard \"no obligation\" language whenever it is absent from a counterparty\'s draft.

**14.3 Unacceptable / Escalate**

> • **Any provision that implies or creates an exclusivity obligation** --- that is, a requirement that either party negotiate exclusively with the other party regarding a specific subject matter, product line, therapeutic area, or transaction during the NDA term or any other period. Exclusivity provisions do not belong in NDAs. An NDA that contains an exclusivity provision effectively converts itself into a partial lock-up agreement and may restrict Stonebridge\'s ability to pursue other strategic opportunities, engage with other potential partners, or respond to unsolicited acquisition proposals. Such provisions must be removed from the NDA. If the counterparty desires exclusivity, it should be negotiated separately as a standalone agreement or as a term within a letter of intent, with appropriate consideration, defined scope, and reasonable time limitations.
>
> • **Any provision that implies a standstill obligation** --- that is, a restriction on either party\'s ability to pursue other transactions involving the other party, acquire equity interests in the other party, propose business combinations, solicit proxies, or take similar actions. Standstill provisions are not addressed in a standalone section of this Playbook because they are not standard NDA terms. If encountered in an NDA, treat any standstill provision as an \"Unacceptable / Escalate\" item and flag for General Counsel\'s immediate attention. Standstill provisions are typically found in M&A-specific confidentiality agreements where one party is a potential acquisition target and the standstill serves as a condition of receiving access to the target\'s confidential information. Even in that context, standstill provisions require careful negotiation regarding scope, duration, and carve-outs, and should be evaluated by General Counsel in coordination with the relevant business lead. Unilateral standstills in mutual NDAs --- that is, standstills that restrict only one party --- are commercially one-sided and atypical outside of M&A-specific contexts where one party is clearly the potential acquirer and the other is clearly the potential target.
>
> • **Any provision that implies an obligation to negotiate or transact** --- that is, language that could be interpreted as a binding agreement to enter into a definitive agreement, to negotiate toward a definitive agreement, or to negotiate in good faith toward a specific outcome. Courts in some jurisdictions have found that \"agreements to agree\" or \"agreements to negotiate\" create enforceable obligations, and Stonebridge should avoid any language that could be construed as such a commitment.

**Commentary:** Exclusivity and standstill provisions belong in letters of intent, term sheets, or definitive agreements --- not in NDAs. Their inclusion in an NDA suggests either a drafting error by the counterparty\'s counsel or a deliberate attempt to obtain concessions that should be negotiated as part of a broader transaction structure with appropriate consideration. The reviewing attorney should flag any such provision immediately and propose its deletion from the NDA. If the counterparty insists on retaining exclusivity, standstill, or negotiation-obligation language, escalate to General Counsel without delay. General Counsel will evaluate whether the provision should be (a) deleted from the NDA and addressed in a separate agreement, (b) accepted with modifications and appropriate consideration, or (c) rejected entirely. Any standstill language in an NDA should be scrutinized particularly closely --- the mere presence of a standstill provision in what is ostensibly a mutual NDA may indicate that the counterparty\'s understanding of the relationship dynamics differs from Stonebridge\'s, which warrants a broader strategic conversation with the business lead.

**[APPENDIX A: ESCALATION PROCEDURES]{.underline}**

**A.1 Overview.** The following escalation procedures apply whenever a provision in a proposed NDA falls into the \"Unacceptable / Escalate\" category as defined in this Playbook, or whenever the reviewing attorney identifies a term that, while potentially within the \"Acceptable Range,\" raises significant concerns in the context of the specific transaction or counterparty relationship.

**A.2 Step-by-Step Escalation Process**

**Step 1: Identification.** The reviewing attorney --- typically David Osei, Associate General Counsel (Commercial), or Mei-Lin Torres, Senior Contracts Manager --- identifies a provision in the proposed NDA that falls into the \"Unacceptable / Escalate\" category based on the criteria established in the relevant section of this Playbook. The reviewing attorney should also identify any provisions that, while technically within the \"Acceptable Range,\" present an elevated risk profile when considered in the context of the overall NDA, the specific counterparty, or the nature of the contemplated transaction.

**Step 2: Preparation of Deviation Summary.** The reviewing attorney prepares a brief deviation summary identifying:

> \(a\) The specific NDA provision at issue, including the section number and relevant language;
>
> \(b\) The corresponding Playbook section and tier classification (i.e., whether the provision falls within \"Preferred Position,\" \"Acceptable Range,\" or \"Unacceptable / Escalate\");
>
> \(c\) The recommended redline or negotiation position --- that is, the specific language changes that would bring the provision within the \"Acceptable Range\" or, ideally, to the \"Preferred Position\"; and
>
> \(d\) A risk assessment rating, using the definitions set forth in Section A.3 below (Critical / High / Medium / Low).

**Step 3: Submission to General Counsel.** The deviation summary is submitted to Patricia Huang, General Counsel, for review. If the issue involves commercial or strategic implications --- for example, a provision that could affect Stonebridge\'s ability to pursue a parallel transaction or that could impact the terms of a potential definitive agreement --- the relevant business lead (e.g., Marcus Ellery, SVP of Corporate Development) should be copied on the submission. The deviation summary should be submitted promptly upon identification of the issue to avoid delays in the negotiation timeline.

**Step 4: General Counsel Determination.** The General Counsel reviews the deviation summary and determines whether to:

> \(a\) **Reject the provision** and instruct the reviewing attorney to propose a redline consistent with Stonebridge\'s Preferred Position or Acceptable Range;
>
> \(b\) **Accept the provision with documented justification** --- in which case the General Counsel will prepare (or direct the preparation of) a risk acceptance memorandum setting forth the reasons for accepting the deviation, the assessed risk level, and any mitigating factors or conditions; or
>
> \(c\) **Escalate further** to the Chief Executive Officer or the Board of Directors if the risk is material to Stonebridge\'s business, intellectual property, or strategic position.

**Step 5: Documentation.** All escalation decisions --- whether the outcome is rejection, conditional acceptance, or further escalation --- must be documented in the matter file for the specific NDA. For material deviations (those rated \"Critical\" or \"High\"), the decision must also be recorded in Stonebridge\'s contract risk register, which is maintained by the Legal Department and reviewed quarterly by the General Counsel.

**A.3 Risk Rating Definitions**

The following risk rating definitions should be used when preparing the deviation summary in Step 2:

**Critical:** The provision creates significant legal exposure, threatens Stonebridge\'s core intellectual property (including patents, trade secrets, and proprietary algorithms), or is fundamentally inconsistent with Stonebridge\'s business interests or risk tolerance. A Critical-rated issue must be resolved --- through redline, deletion, or renegotiation --- before the NDA is executed. Execution of an NDA with an unresolved Critical issue requires express written approval from the General Counsel and documentation in a risk acceptance memorandum.

**High:** The provision is outside the Acceptable Range as defined in this Playbook and creates meaningful legal, commercial, or operational risk for Stonebridge. There is a strong recommendation to redline the provision. A High-rated issue may be accepted only with General Counsel approval and a documented justification explaining why acceptance is appropriate in light of the specific transaction context and risk-mitigation measures.

**Medium:** The provision is below the Preferred Position but within or near the boundary of the Acceptable Range. The reviewing attorney should negotiate toward the Preferred Position where possible, but the provision may be accepted if the overall deal balance is favorable and the deviation does not create undue risk when considered in the context of the NDA as a whole. Medium-rated deviations should be noted in the matter file but do not require formal General Counsel approval.

**Low:** A minor deviation from the Preferred Position that falls clearly within the Acceptable Range. The reviewing attorney should note the deviation for the record and, if convenient, attempt to negotiate toward the Preferred Position, but a Low-rated deviation is unlikely to warrant a contested redline or escalation.

**A.4 Practical Considerations**

Business leads should be aware that provisions falling into the \"Unacceptable / Escalate\" category will require escalation and may delay execution timelines. This should be factored into deal planning and communication with counterparties. In general, Stonebridge\'s negotiators should inform counterparties early in the negotiation process that certain terms are outside Stonebridge\'s policy parameters, to manage expectations and avoid eleventh-hour disputes.

The escalation process is designed to ensure consistency and accountability across Stonebridge\'s NDA practice. It also creates an institutional record that can be used to identify patterns in counterparty behavior, track the frequency and nature of deviations, and refine this Playbook over time.

**Last Updated:** January 15, 2025

The Playbook is available to business leads upon request, subject to General Counsel approval.

**Confidentiality Notice:** This document is confidential and intended solely for internal use by authorized personnel of Stonebridge Medical Devices, Inc. Do not distribute this document to counterparties, outside counsel, or any other third parties without the prior written approval of the General Counsel.   "The omission of the independent-development exclusion is the single most consequential gap for Stonebridge’s R&D. item(id="C-3", rating="Critical", title="Exclusive arbitration with express waiver of court access; no injunctive-relief clause",

  "§9.1 is materially worse than a mere omission: it affirmatively and irrevocably waives the right to seek any court relief, including emergency relief.  esc="Escalate to General Counsel immediately if Veridian will not delete the court-access waiver and add the carve-out (Playbook §8.3 commentary).")

item(id="C-4", rating="Critical", title="German governing law; ICC arbitration seated in Zurich",

 pb="Playbook §7.1 (Preferred: Delaware law; exclusive jurisdiction of Delaware Court of Chancery, or D. Del.); §7.2 (Acceptable: New York law with Manhattan state/federal courts; or AAA Commercial Arbitration seated in a neutral U.S. city); §7.3 (Unacceptable: foreign governing law — German law expressly named; foreign seat — Zurich expressly named; ICC; any non-U.S. dispute resolution). Tier: **Unacceptable / Escalate** on four independent grounds.",
 analysis=[
  "§8 triggers each of the four separate “Unacceptable” bullets in Playbook §7.3. The Playbook states that Stonebridge “should not agree to any non-U.S. forum under any circumstances absent General Counsel approval,” and that any such approval “would be exceptional and would require a documented risk acceptance memorandum.”",
  "Substantive concerns specific to this draft: (i) German law applies different default rules on implied rights in disclosed technical information, and the draft is silent on IP ownership (item C-9) — the Playbook (§10.3) flags exactly this combination; (ii) the enforceability under German law of several Veridian-favorable clauses (e.g., the unilateral no-hire in §7, the standstill in §15) and of Stonebridge-favorable protections would have to be analyzed by German counsel at additional cost; (iii) ICC fees and a Zurich seat materially increase the cost and time of any enforcement action, which, combined with the €5,000,000 cap (item C-5) and the costs rule in §8.2 (each Party bears its own fees), could make pursuing a breach uneconomic.",
  "Veridian’s counsel has emphasized that the form is “vetted for consistency with applicable European and U.S. confidentiality frameworks” and that his firm has a New York office. Those points support, rather than undermine, a neutral U.S. compromise: New York law with New York courts or AAA arbitration in New York is a familiar cross-border solution that the Playbook (§7.3 commentary) specifically identifies as the compromise to offer."],
 redline="8.1 Governing Law.   "Unlike boilerplate limitation clauses that can be fixed with a carve-out, §13.1 is drafted to target confidentiality breaches specifically: it names “damages arising from breach of confidentiality obligations,” lost profits and lost business opportunity — the categories that represent essentially all of the real harm from a leak of trade secrets or regulatory data (Playbook §13.3). Recovery would be confined to direct out-of-pocket loss, and then capped at €5,000,000 in aggregate for all claims.",
  "The cap is disproportionate to the value at risk. Stonebridge has approximately $485 million in annual revenue, 87 active U.S. patents, and proprietary micro-needle fabrication processes and predictive dosing algorithms that underpin its insulin delivery platform. The Playbook is explicit that any cap, “whether … one million dollars or one hundred million dollars,” is unacceptable for confidentiality breaches because it pre-discounts the cost of a breach.",
  "Because the NDA’s only substantive obligations are confidentiality, non-use, return/destruction and the restrictive covenants, a cap-with-carve-out structure would leave the cap applying almost exclusively to Stonebridge’s own exposure under Veridian’s restrictive covenants (§§7, 14, 15). The cleanest outcome is deletion of §13 in full (Playbook §13.2).",
  "The final sentence of §11.1 is ambiguous: read literally, “neither Party shall be liable for any damages arising from the use of … any Confidential Information” could be invoked by a Receiving Party to escape liability for its own misuse. item(id="C-6", rating="Critical", title="Unilateral standstill binding only Stonebridge",

 quote="§15.1: “During the Term and for a period of twelve (12) months following the expiration or termination of this Agreement, Stonebridge shall not … (a) acquire … any voting securities of Veridian or any of its Affiliates; (b) seek or propose any merger … ; (c) … solicitation of proxies … ; (d) form, join … a ‘group’ (within the meaning of Section 13(d)(3) of the … Securities Exchange Act of 1934) … ; or (e) take any action that would reasonably be expected to require Veridian … to make a public announcement …”",

item(id="C-8", rating="Critical", title="“Representatives” limited to employees and in-house counsel; outside advisors subject to sole-discretion consent; Affiliates barred",
 nda="§1.2; §4.2; §4.3; §4.4",
 quote="§1.2: “‘Representatives’ means … the employees and in-house legal counsel of such Party …” §4.3: prior written approval required before disclosure to “any financial advisors, accountants, auditors, or consultants,” the request must “identify the specific advisor or consultant,” and the Disclosing Party “shall have sole discretion to grant or deny any such request.” §4.4: disclosure to Affiliates “is prohibited without the prior written consent of the Disclosing Party,” which may be conditioned on a joinder.",
 pb="Playbook §11.1 (Preferred: officers, directors, employees, agents, advisors, consultants and Affiliates; Affiliate control at 50% or more); §11.3 (Unacceptable: definition “limited to ‘employees and in-house legal counsel’” — named expressly; excludes Affiliates; excludes agents and consultants); §4.1 (outside-advisor access is “non-negotiable”); §4.3 (Acceptable: advisor consent only if “not … unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed”); §4.4 (Unacceptable: consent in “sole discretion”; requirement to name recipients in advance). Tier: **Unacceptable / Escalate**.",
 analysis=[
  "The draft reproduces almost verbatim the definition the Playbook singles out as “functionally unacceptable” (§11.3). Read together, §§1.2 and 4.2–4.4 would prevent Stonebridge from sharing Veridian information with: its directors and officers who are not “employees” (including the Board, which may need to approve any co-development); its outside counsel Northgate Whitford LLP (outside counsel is not covered at all — §4.3 does not even list legal counsel); its financial advisor Harmon Steele & Associates and accountants Clearview Accounting Group except with Veridian’s sole-discretion approval; technical and regulatory consultants who would evaluate Veridian’s formulation; and any Stonebridge Affiliate or subsidiary.",
  "The sole-discretion consent gives Veridian a veto over Stonebridge’s diligence process (Playbook §4.4), and the requirement to identify the specific advisor, the information and the purpose in advance is impractical as advisor teams change (Playbook §4.4).",
  "Mutuality does not cure the problem: Stonebridge, not Veridian, is the party that relies heavily on external advisors in transaction evaluations. The existing safeguards — need-to-know, written confidentiality obligations and Stonebridge’s responsibility for its Representatives under §5.3 — already protect Veridian."],
 redline="1.2 “Representatives” means, with respect to a Party, [-the employees and in-house legal counsel of such Party-]{+such Party’s and its Affiliates’ respective directors, officers, employees, agents, consultants and professional advisors (including legal counsel, accountants, auditors and financial advisors)+} who have a need to know the Confidential Information in connection with the Purpose.\n\n1.3 “Affiliate” means … where “control” means the direct or indirect ownership of [-more than fifty percent (50%)-]{+fifty percent (50%) or more+} of the outstanding voting securities or equivalent ownership interest of such entity.\n\n4.2 … and who are bound by written confidentiality obligations {+(or, in the case of legal counsel and accountants, professional duties of confidentiality)+} at least as restrictive as those contained in this Agreement. …\n\n[-4.3 Prior written approval of the Disclosing Party shall be required before … [delete in full] … sole discretion to grant or deny any such request.-]\n\n[-4.4 Disclosure of Confidential Information to Affiliates of the Receiving Party is prohibited without the prior written consent of the Disclosing Party. … [delete in full].-]",

 esc="Escalate to General Counsel if Veridian refuses to expand the definition to, at minimum, employees, officers, directors and professional advisors (Playbook §11.3), or insists on sole-discretion consent (Playbook §4.4).")

item(id="H-3", rating="High", title="Seven-year survival of all confidentiality obligations (no trade-secret tail)",
 nda="§3.2 (Survival); §3.1 (Term)",
 quote="§3.2: confidentiality and non-use obligations “shall survive the expiration or termination of this Agreement for a period of seven (7) years following the date of such expiration or termination …” §3.1: Term of three (3) years, terminable by either Party on 30 days’ notice.",
 pb="Playbook §1.1 (Preferred: 2-year term; 3-year survival); §1.2 (Acceptable: 1–3-year term; 2–5-year survival; document rationale above 3 years); §1.3 (Unacceptable: survival exceeding five years; perpetual obligations acceptable only if limited to trade secrets). Tier: **Unacceptable / Escalate** (survival); term is within Acceptable Range (see L-2).",
 analysis=[
  "Seven years of survival exceeds the five-year ceiling in Playbook §1.3; the Playbook commentary notes that six- or seven-year periods are commonly proposed by life-sciences counterparties and treats them as disproportionate absent exceptional circumstances. Because the clock starts at expiration of a three-year Term, obligations on early disclosures could run for roughly ten years, imposing long tracking and compliance burdens on Stonebridge as Receiving Party.",
  "Nuance for the negotiation: the obligations are mutual, and Stonebridge will itself disclose highly sensitive micro-needle and dosing information. The right answer is therefore not simply a shorter period, but a period within the Acceptable Range plus a perpetual tail limited to trade secrets (expressly permitted by Playbook §1.3) — which gives Stonebridge’s core technology better protection than Veridian’s flat seven years, because trade secrets would be protected for as long as they remain secret.",
  "Recommended counter: five years’ survival (justified by the co-development nature, clinical and regulatory data — Playbook §1.2 commentary; record the rationale in the matter file), plus trade-secret protection for so long as the information remains a trade secret. Opening at the preferred three years is possible but is unlikely to be credible against Veridian’s seven."],
 redline="3.2 The obligations of confidentiality and non-use set forth in this Agreement, including without limitation the obligations contained in Sections 4, 5, and 6, shall survive the expiration or termination of this Agreement for a period of [-seven (7)-]{+five (5)+} years following the date of such expiration or termination, regardless of the reason for such expiration or termination{+; provided, however, that with respect to any Confidential Information that constitutes a trade secret under applicable law (including the Defend Trade Secrets Act, 18 U.S.C. § 1836 et seq.), such obligations shall survive for so long as such Confidential Information remains a trade secret under applicable law+}. For the avoidance of doubt, the survival of such obligations shall apply to all Confidential Information disclosed during the Term {+(or prior to the Effective Date in connection with the Purpose)+}, irrespective of when during the Term such disclosure occurred.",
 fallback="Any survival period of 2–5 years plus the trade-secret tail is within the Acceptable Range (Playbook §1.2). A perpetual obligation for all Confidential Information, or survival beyond five years for non-trade-secret information, requires General Counsel approval.",
 esc="Escalate to General Counsel if Veridian will not come to five years or less (Playbook §1.3 commentary).")

item(id="H-4", rating="High", title="Oral/visual disclosures: 5-business-day written confirmation with automatic forfeiture; key categories omitted",
 nda="§1.1 (Confidential Information), both paragraphs",
 quote="“… information disclosed orally or visually shall constitute Confidential Information only if the Disclosing Party provides written confirmation … within five (5) business days … Failure to provide such written confirmation within the five (5) business day period shall result in such orally or visually disclosed information being deemed non-confidential for purposes of this Agreement.” The enumerated list omits regulatory filings and source code.",
 pb="Playbook §2.1 (Preferred: written information marked; oral/visual identified at disclosure and confirmed in writing within 10 business days; must enumerate technical data, financial information, business plans, customer lists, regulatory filings and source code); §2.2 (Acceptable: confirmation window up to 30 calendar days; “reasonable particularity” standard); §2.3 (Unacceptable: window shorter than 10 business days paired with rigid forfeiture). Tier: **Unacceptable / Escalate** (forfeiture); omissions to be redlined.",
 analysis=[
  "The five-business-day window with automatic forfeiture is precisely the combination Playbook §2.3 prohibits. It is especially dangerous here because the most sensitive exchange — the May 19, 2025 technical kickoff in Munich, likely including demonstrations, white-boarding and lab or prototype review — will be oral and visual. Unless Stonebridge’s technical team delivered detailed written confirmations by Monday, May 26, 2025, everything Stonebridge showed in Munich would be “deemed non-confidential.” The forfeiture is mutual on its face, but Stonebridge, as the owner of the device and fabrication know-how being demonstrated, bears most of the risk.",
  "The enumerated categories omit “regulatory filings” and “source code” (both mandatory under Playbook §2.1), even though Veridian’s counsel’s cover email itself describes the exchange of “regulatory filings” as a purpose of the NDA. Stonebridge’s FDA submissions (510(k)/PMA data), firmware and predictive dosing algorithms must be expressly listed.",

 analysis=[
  "Transfers of personal data (e.g., patient-level clinical data, employee information) from Veridian in Germany to Stonebridge in Minnesota would be subject to the EU General Data Protection Regulation, including its restrictions on transfers to third countries (Chapter V), and may require Standard Contractual Clauses or another transfer mechanism. Receiving such data without a compliant framework creates regulatory exposure for both parties and potential liability for Stonebridge as recipient.",
  "For an evaluation-stage NDA the simplest solution is a covenant that personal data will not be disclosed (other than business contact details), and that any clinical data shared will be anonymized, unless the parties first sign an appropriate data-transfer agreement."],
 redline="Insert new §4.5: {+4.5 Personal Data. # Part 1 executive summary
heading(doc, "1. Executive Summary", 1)
para(doc, "Veridian’s counsel presents the draft as “balanced and reflective of market-standard practice” and states that Veridian “does not typically accept material modifications.” Measured against the Playbook, the draft is neither balanced nor market-standard for a mutual evaluation NDA. It departs from the Playbook in 14 of the 14 Playbook term categories (Section 13 indemnification aside, which is acceptable by silence) and adds two provisions — an M&A-style standstill and an exclusivity lock-up — that the Playbook says do not belong in an NDA at all. Several provisions are expressly one-directional in Veridian’s favor.")
para(doc, "**The most serious issues, in priority order:**", space_after=3)
for t in [
 "**IP leakage (C-1, C-2, C-9).** A broad residuals clause (§5.4) lets Veridian personnel use retained “know-how, methodologies, and techniques” for “any purpose,” with no IP carve-out; there is no independent-development exclusion; and the agreement is silent on IP ownership/no license — under German law. Together these put Stonebridge’s micro-needle fabrication processes and predictive dosing algorithms at direct risk during the Munich technical kickoff.",
 "**No effective enforcement (C-3, C-4, C-5).** All disputes go to ICC arbitration seated in Zurich under German law; §9.1 irrevocably waives any court action (so no TRO or preliminary injunction); and §13 waives consequential damages expressly for confidentiality breaches and caps all liability at €5,000,000.",
 "**Deal-structure terms disguised as boilerplate (C-6, C-7).** A one-way standstill (§15) bars Stonebridge from proposing any transaction with Veridian for up to four years; §14.1 imposes three-year mutual exclusivity across all transdermal insulin co-development, co-marketing and co-manufacturing. These are strategic issues for General Counsel and Corporate Development.",
 "**Operational blockers (C-8, H-4).** “Representatives” is limited to employees and in-house counsel (excluding directors, officers, outside counsel, Harmon Steele, Clearview, consultants and Affiliates, subject only to Veridian’s sole-discretion consent); oral/visual disclosures are forfeited unless confirmed within five business days — a trap for the May 19 kickoff.",
 "**One-sided covenants and mechanics (H-1, H-2, H-3, H-5, H-6).** Unilateral 24-month no-hire on Stonebridge; free assignment for Veridian only; seven-year survival; “immediate” compelled-disclosure notice with no cooperation duty; 90-day return with no certification and an unconditioned archival copy."]:
    bullet(doc, t)
para(doc, "**Recommendation.** (1) Submit this report to the General Counsel now for the Critical/High items (Part 6). (2) Respond to Mr. Brenner promptly with a full redline on Veridian’s paper (to respect its form) and a short issues list framed around mutuality and market practice, offering the concessions identified in Part 5. (3) Instruct Marcus Ellery and the technical team that no Stonebridge confidential information is to be shared — including at or before the May 19 kickoff — until a compliant NDA is signed. The May 9 deadline is achievable only if Veridian engages on the Critical items in the week of April 28.", space_after=8)

counts = {}

 ["Critical", str(counts.get("Critical", 0)), "Must be resolved before execution; execution with an unresolved item requires GC written approval and a risk acceptance memorandum."],
 ["High", str(counts.get("High", 0)), "Outside Acceptable Range; strong recommendation to redline; acceptance only with GC approval and documented justification."],

], [Inches(1.9), Inches(0.6), Inches(4.0)], size=9, rating_col=None)

# Part 2 context
heading(doc, "2. Context from Veridian Counsel’s Email (April 22, 2025)", 1)
for t in [
 "**Deal setting.** Exploratory co-development of a next-generation transdermal insulin patch combining Stonebridge’s micro-needle array technology with Veridian’s transdermal formulation expertise, following the April 14, 2025 meeting of Dr. Richter and Marcus Ellery in Barcelona. The NDA is intended to cover “confidential technical data, financial projections, and regulatory filings.” Stonebridge’s most valuable assets (micro-needle fabrication processes, predictive dosing algorithms, firmware) are directly in scope, which is why the IP-protection items are rated Critical.",
 "**Timing pressure.** Execution is requested by May 9 so that “unrestricted data sharing” can occur at the May 19 Munich kickoff. Playbook Appendix A.4 anticipates that Unacceptable terms will require escalation and may delay timelines; the counterparty should be told early. The timing pressure should not be allowed to drive acceptance of Critical terms; Part 6 proposes a timeline and a contingency for May 19.",
 "**Negotiating posture.** “Veridian does not typically accept material modifications” is an opening position; counsel also says Veridian is “entirely open to discussing” specific provisions. Our response should (i) acknowledge Veridian’s form and work within it; (ii) emphasize that most of our changes are mutual and protect Veridian equally (independent development, no-license, injunctive relief, compelled-disclosure cooperation, residuals); and (iii) explain that the standstill, exclusivity, one-way non-solicit and one-way assignment are not features of a mutual NDA and contradict the email’s own description of the form as “balanced.”",
 "**Inconsistency to note.** The draft’s claim of consistency with “U.S. confidentiality frameworks” sits uneasily with an irrevocable waiver of court access (which would forfeit Defend Trade Secrets Act injunctive and seizure remedies) and with the omission of the independent-development exclusion that is standard in U.S. practice.",
 "**Administrative points.** The Kramer, Hecht & Wollstein address in the NDA notice clause (Maximilianstraße 35) differs from Mr. Brenner’s signature block (Maximilianstraße 28) — clarify (L-3). Veridian’s team has separately told Mr. Ellery to expect the NDA; Mr. Ellery should route any business-channel discussion of NDA terms through Legal and should not signal acceptance of the form."]:
    bullet(doc, t)
